name: Reinforce a squad
summary: A unit made of several bodies, its own squad or a crew of AI followers tied to it, gets lost bodies back in the field without being bought again. In the squad form each lost member is replaced one at a time, for a price and a short wait, near a friendly base, a held point or a teammate's vehicle that doubles as a reinforcement point; a squad with nobody left can't be topped up, so players pull a hurt squad back to save the last member and everything it has earned. In the follower form, separate AI followers (workers or escorts) come back by themselves at their master after a delay, free and up to a cap, until the master dies. Either way, damage that neither wipes the group nor removes its source is only temporary.
counterplay: Wipe the whole group: a squad with no survivors can't be topped up, so chase down the last members before they reach a source.
Take away the source: destroy the reinforcing vehicle or point, push the squad away from it, or block call-ins.
Punish the refill: new members arrive one at a time and cost money, so push while the squad is still rebuilding.
Against respawning followers, go for the master: killing followers only buys a delay, and the master's death ends the stream.
Strike in the gap right after the followers fall and before they return, when the unit is at its weakest.
Use splash: bunched members die together.

other_examples.unit: Infantry squad reinforcement (all armies), M3 Halftrack and Reinforcement Point
other_examples.note: Every soldier in a squad is hit and killed separately, and a missing man is replaced one click at a time for a fraction of the squad's price, usually only within range of the headquarters, a reinforcing building or a vehicle such as the US halftrack, which works as a mobile reinforcement point even in enemy ground. A squad never grows past its starting size (bar one Panzer Elite upgrade), and one with nobody left is gone for good, so players order a retreat to save the last man and the veterancy he carries. Panzer Elite troops can also turn a neutral building into a reinforcement point that any Axis player's infantry may use.

sources.title: M3 Halftrack, Company of Heroes Wiki
Reinforcement Point, Company of Heroes Wiki

other_examples.note: A fast transport whose second job is being a reinforcement point with a small radius: squads close to it top up without going home, and in team games allied players' squads can use it as well. It heals nothing, so reinforcing a badly hurt squad mid-fight wastes money.

other_examples.unit: Infantry squads, Medic and Medic Station (all factions)
other_examples.note: Squads are topped up and healed back at base after a retreat, but a medic squad that has reached veteran rank can give itself up to plant a medic station anywhere on the map: a forward spot where damaged squads reinforce instead of walking home. The medics cannot replace lost men themselves. Both medic pages carry the wiki's beta banner, so this needs a check against the final game.

sources.title: Polanian Medic, Iron Harvest Wiki
sources.note: Says the medics of all factions work the same way; marked as a beta page.

shooter_analogues.note: For contrast (the squad crew this pattern acts on, without the refill): in a first-person shooter, each player fields a squad of three to nine AI soldiers, plays one of them and can give the others orders or switch to them. The page read shows no way to top a squad up during a life.

The follower form in an action game: a passive skill keeps up to seven skeletons at the necromancer's side and raises a new one every couple of seconds while any are missing; the active part sends them all at one target for extra damage.
An item gives the player two allied probes that fight beside them and are summoned again half a minute after being destroyed, at no cost.

sources.title: Empathy Cores, Risk of Rain 2 Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: For contrast (closer to host-spawn-point and drop-in-from-above): a living player calls a dead teammate back down in a drop pod, from a limited pool of uses that grows with the squad's size; jammers block the call, and the landing pod can hurt enemies where it comes down.

player_translation.summary: A player who leads a small group, a squad of AI soldiers or a crew of AI followers tied to their unit, and keeps it at strength in the field. Lost members come back near a friendly source or at the unit itself, so the enemy must wipe the group or kill its source to make the damage count.
as_user: You buy a squad: you play its leader, and three or four AI followers move with you and shoot at what you shoot, so your firepower and staying power grow with every member you keep alive.

Losses weaken you without killing you: inside the ring of a friendly source (the spawn, a held point or a teammate's transport) hold Q to bring back one lost follower. Each costs a little money and a few seconds, and the new member runs in from the source.
When the squad is nearly gone the smart play is to pull back: while anyone lives, rebuilding is cheaper than a new purchase and you keep any ranks.
With the respawning-followers variant there is no key: your followers come back at you one by one, free, after a delay, so your job is to stay alive and guard them while they work or fight.
as_target: Damage on a squad only sticks if you finish it: the nameplate shows how many members are left, so you know when a last push will wipe it.
A refilling squad is weakest while new members trickle in; hit it then, or catch it on the walk back to its source.
Find and kill the source: a transport or point that feeds squads shows a reinforcement ring.
Against followers, aim at the master; their respawn timers show how long you have before they return.
teammates: A teammate's transport or vehicle becomes a mobile reinforcement point, so squads stay with it and infantry and vehicles push together.
Allies can top up at each other's sources, which makes running a reinforcing vehicle a support job in its own right.
Healers restore health while reinforcement restores bodies, so the two work together.
On the enemy side, splash and area-damage picks become the answer to bunched squads.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; left mouse fires the leader's weapon, and the followers fire at the leader's target.
Hold Q inside a friendly source's ring to call back one lost follower; this is the pattern's one counted key, and the hold breaks if the leader takes heavy fire.
Respawning-followers variant: passive, no key. An optional order (send every follower at the target under the cursor) would be a counted key on Q.
Middle mouse, the universal ping, on a transport: 'need reinforcement'.
feedback: A squad strip in the HUD with a pip per follower that empties when one dies and refills with a timer or a price.
Reinforcement sources show a team-coloured ring when a squad that can refill is near, and a runner or a drop shows the new member arriving.
The nameplate shows the squad's size (such as 4/5) to everyone, so enemies can read how close it is to being wiped.
Respawning followers: a countdown icon over the master for each follower on its way back.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS one player runs many squads; here one player is one squad, so followers need no micromanagement: they follow, take cover near the leader and fire at the leader's target.
RTS reinforcement is a menu click; here it is a held key inside a visible ring, so enemies can see it and punish it.
Losing the whole squad also loses its veterancy in Company of Heroes; keeping that rule makes the last-member retreat a real decision.
A free, automatic respawn like the Slave Miner's needs a readable timer and a cap, or the followers feel unkillable.
In Red Alert 2 the freed slaves join the side that killed the miner; that twist is fun but confusing, so it stays a high-spice variant.

team_play.notes: A squad needs a source to refill, so it sticks to a teammate's transport or a held point, which turns that teammate into a forward base; the enemy has to bring splash and focus to wipe groups or hunt down the source.

notes: Several AI bodies per player: following, formation, cover and shared targets, all simulated and networked in a browser game.
Hit detection on every body, and a clear rule for what happens when the leader falls while followers live.
Sources: rings on vehicles and points, costs, timers and the arrival of new members.
The follower form adds jobs for the followers (working or guarding) and a respawn timer per follower.
Topping up mid-fight can make a squad outlast its price; costs, a held key and a visible ring keep it honest.
Free respawning followers can soak fire forever; cap their number and give them a long, visible timer.
Several guns under one player can out-damage a single unit of the same tier, so followers' weapons stay weak.
From above, players must tell the leader from its followers, and followers from enemy players.
The group's size, the source in use and each follower's respawn timer all need to be visible.
Followers that change sides (the turncoat variant) are confusing unless their colour changes at once.

variants.name: Reinforce at a source
variants.summary: Replace lost members one at a time, for a small price and a short wait, inside the ring of a friendly spawn, held point or reinforcing vehicle; a wiped squad can't be topped up.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes squads with the M3 Halftrack and Panzer Elite reinforcement points; Dawn of War II Razorback

variants.name: Reinforce anywhere
variants.summary: Members can be replaced anywhere, but each one takes longer or costs more and arrives from above or from the map edge.
variants.seen_in: Dawn of War II's global drop-pod reinforcement, named on the Razorback strategy page

adds_weaknesses.why: Each replacement costs more or takes longer than at a friendly point, and a squad wiped out entirely is gone with everything it earned.

variants.name: Be the reinforcement point
variants.summary: A vehicle that doubles as a reinforcement point: squads near it, teammates' included, top up their losses without walking back, and it may carry them as well.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes M3 Halftrack; Dawn of War II Razorback, which allies can also use

adds_strengths.why: Squads near it, its teammates' included, top up their losses without walking back to base.

adds_weaknesses.why: It has to stay near the infantry it feeds, which puts a support vehicle close to the front.

countered_by.why: Killing the reinforcing vehicle cuts off every squad that relies on it.

variants.name: Plant a reinforcement post
variants.summary: On a key, set up a forward post (by claiming a building, or by giving up the unit itself) where squads, teammates' included, can top up their losses until the enemy destroys or retakes it.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes Panzer Elite reinforcement points in converted buildings; Iron Harvest veteran medics' medic station

adds_strengths.why: Gives its team a forward spot to top up squads, so infantry stay at the front instead of walking home.

adds_weaknesses.why: The post stands still and is easy to find; once it is destroyed or retaken, the squads that relied on it lose their refill.

countered_by.why: Artillery levels a fixed post from out of reach.

variants.name: Respawning followers
variants.summary: The bodies are separate AI followers tied to the unit, a work crew or an escort, rather than its own members: each one lost comes back at the unit by itself after a delay, free, up to a cap, and the whole crew ends when the unit dies.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Slave Miner (worker slaves); Diablo III Command Skeletons; Risk of Rain 2 Empathy Cores

adds_strengths.why: Its followers come back by themselves and for free, so killing them only buys a delay.

adds_weaknesses.why: Its followers are soft and work or fight away from it, and its own death ends the whole crew.

countered_by.why: Fast-firing anti-infantry weapons keep the soft followers down and stop their work.
Flankers slip past the crew and go straight for the master, which ends every follower at once.

variants.name: Turncoat followers
variants.summary: As respawning followers, but when the master dies its followers switch to the killer's side for the rest of their lives, so killing it pays twice; they can no longer do their old job.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Slave Miner, whose freed slaves join whoever destroyed it

adds_strengths.why: Its followers come back by themselves and for free, so killing them only buys a delay.

adds_weaknesses.why: When it dies its whole crew joins the side that killed it, so losing it feeds the enemy.

countered_by.why: Fast-firing anti-infantry weapons keep the soft followers down and stop their work.
Flankers go straight for the master and are rewarded with its freed crew.

adds_strengths.why: Lost members come back in the field, so damage that doesn't wipe the squad is only temporary.

adds_weaknesses.why: Topping up needs a friendly source, money and a few seconds, and a squad wiped out entirely is gone with everything it earned.

counters.why: Picking off one member at a time barely dents a squad that refills between shots.

countered_by.why: Splash kills bunched members together and can wipe the squad before it reaches a source.
Fast flankers hunt down the reinforcing vehicle or catch a hurt squad on its way back.

open_questions: Will Shamble Frontlines have squad units at all? If so, what happens when the leader falls while followers live: does the squad die, or does the player take over a follower?
Should topping up cost team money, the player's own money, or only time?
Respawning followers: free with a long timer (as on the Slave Miner) or a small cost each? And should the turncoat twist exist at all, since it makes AI units change sides mid-fight?
Where may a squad refill: only at the spawn, at held points, at teammates' transports, or anywhere for a longer wait?

shooter_fit.reason: Squads of AI soldiers already work in a shooter (Enlisted) and self-respawning pets in action games (Diablo III, Risk of Rain 2), but several bodies per player strain top-down readability and browser networking.

review.notes: Re-checked field by field against its sources by the batch r1 checker, which covered all 33 batch patterns; research/r1/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. Nothing was found wrong.
